ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Repeal of Armed Forces Special Powers Act 
*301. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA : Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are considering a proposal to repeal the Armed 
Forces Special Powers Act from entire Manipur as a major step to restore 
normalcy and peace in the N.E. Region; 
(b) whether the view-point of the State Government of Manipur has been 
ascertained in this regard; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and the response of the State Government 
thereto? 
THE MINJSTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI S. REGUPATHY): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House: 
Statement 
Following the demands made by the general public and civil groups, a 
Committee headed by Justice B.P Jeev an Reddy, former Judge of the 
Supreme Court of India has been constituted on 19/11/2004 to review the 
Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958 as amended in 1972 Dr. S.B. 
Nakade, former Vice Chancellor and Juris t; Shri P.P. Srivastava, IAS(Retd.), 
former Special Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs; Lt. Gen. (Retd.) V.R. 
Reghavan, former Director General Military Operation and Shri Sanjoy 
Hazarika, Journalist are the members of this Co mmittee. The Committee 
would review the provisions of the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 
1958 as amended in 1972 and advise whether— 
1

RAJYA SABHA [22 December, 2004] 
(a) To amend the provisions of the Act to bring them in consonance 
with the obligations of the Government towards protection of 
Human Rights; or 
(b) To replace the. Act by a more humane Act. 
In connection with the review of the Armed Forces (Special Powers) 
Act, 1958 as amended in 1972, the Committee may interact with individuals, 
representatives of social groups, St ate Governments of the North Eastern 
region and concerned agencies of Central Government as deemed 
necessary by the Committee. The Co mmittee would submit its report 
within a period of six months. 
SHR! MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Sir, my first supplementary is 
whether 
it is a fact that in Manipur the Ar med Forces (Special Powers) Act has 
been invoked for over two decades. My  humble question to the hon. Minister 
is whether the number of insurgent groups, after the promulgation of the 
Act, has increased manifold during these two decades and whether the 
number of people involved in insurgency or the number of those insurgent 
groups has increased manifold. 
This is part (a) of my first supplementary. 
Part (b) of my first supplementary is  whether the civil society of Manipur 
is very badly sandwiched between the excess of the Armed Forces and 
the excess of the insurgent groups. Would you kindly reply to this? 
SHRIS. REGUPATHY: Hon. Chairman, Sir, there are 23 insurgent groups 
active in the State. Of that, 7 have be en declared as unl awful association. 
Insurgency in Manipur is broadly in three areas. They are Naga insurgency 
in hill districts, Metei insurgency in the valley and Kuki insurgency in the 
lower reaches of the hill districts. At the-same time, due to the Armed 
Forces (Special Powers) Act, which is in force, now the ground level 
situation 
is under control. 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Mr. Minister, you have not 
understood 
my question. My question was very specific, whether the number of 
insurgent groups and the number of people involved in insurgency had 
gone up during the last 20 years. 
SHRI S. REGUPATHY: In  the present year, it is less. We are talking 
about 2004. It is less this year. 
2 

[22 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: I have not asked about the present 
year. I have asked whether it has gone up manifold in the last 20 years. 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL): Sir, 
the number of insurgent groups has gone up. But to say that the civil 
society is sandwiched between the police and the insurgents will not be 
correct because the police are protectin g the innocent, their lives and their 
limbs. Sometimes, if mistakes happen, it does not mean that the police 
are not protecting the civil society. When we had gone there, we were told 
by some groups of persons and some representatives of some societies 
that this law and the police should always be there to protect them. 
SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: My second supplementary to the 
hon. 
Minister, through you, Sir, is whether a considerable number of young 
boys and girls in Manipur fell victims to police or Armed Forces atrocities 
in the popular agitation demanding withdrawal of the Armed Forces (Spe- 
cial Powers) Act from Manipur during the period 12th July to mid August. 
The hon. Home Minister was there on 5th August, if I remember correctly, 
and he tried to control the situation. My question is whether the Govern- 
ment of India is taking some palliative measures or confidence building 
measures to compensate those victim s of the popular democratic agita- 
tion for withdrawal of the Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act from Manipur. 
I know that a number of people had been very badly injured. I have seen 
the video clippings. By and large, the people were peaceful in their agita- 
tion. Some boys like Pebam Chittaranjan did self-immolation. A number of 
boys and girls were victims. They were lodged in the Jawaharlal Nehru 
Hospital where the hon. Home Minister, perhaps visited. Some were lodged 
in RIMS. There was a very serious s ituation. Still the people are bearing 
the brunt of the situation. Would the Minister kindly respond to this? 
SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL: We would like to be sympathetic to all the 
people in Manipur who need sympathy and who should be helped. But 
these are questions which can be examined very carefully so as to take 
proper action. If there are cases in wh ich some people have been attacked 
or arrested or put behind bars, wrongly, that is a different issue. But it will 
be difficult for me to say that we will make a policy and say that all those 
who are involved in it will be compensated. The State Government has 
also to be consulted in these matters. 
SHRI SHANKAR ROY CHOWDHURY: Sir, would the Minister be kind 
enough to inform us, when a Central Police Organisation like the CRPF or 
a Para-Military Force like the BSF are deployed to aid the civil authorities, 
from where they derived their powers to arrest, search and open fire? 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [22 December, 2004] 
SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL: Of course, under the law which has been 
discussed and that is why the Government has been very careful. The 
Government has to take into consideration the demands made by some 
people as well as the requirement to  see that help and assistance is 
provided to the innocent people by the Armed Forces. So, this is an issue 
which has to be considered in a very, very balanced manner in order to 
take a decision. And this is exactly what we are trying to do. 
SHRI MATILAL SARKAR: Sir, I would like to know whether the hon. 
Minister has made any estimate of the extent of excesses committed by 
some of the Army personnel during the agitation period and whether any 
punitive measures have been taken against the guilty personnel of the 
Army. 
SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL: Well, if there are any such cases in which 
there is a scope for proceeding against the people who have taken action, 
these are matters which have to be ve ry carefully assessed by the authori- 
ties in the State and then the matters have to be taken to the court for 
decisions to be given. We would not be in a position to say that all-those 
who were trying to maintain law and order and trying to help the innocent 
people are guilty.

THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELAV 
(a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Yes, Sir. There has been a significant increase in imports of 
raw silk and silk fabric from China. From 2001-2002 to 2003-2004 raw silk 
imports have risen by 74.8% and silk fabric by 1571.8% These imports 
have come in at prices lower than the domestic prices, causing distress 
to domestic industry. 
(d) Major steps taken by the Government of India to protect domestic 
silk industry are given below:— 
(i) Antidumping duty has been imposed by the Government of 
India with effect from 2nd January, 2003 on all imported 
mullberry 
raw silk (not thrown) of international grade 2A and below, 
originated in or exported from People's Republic of China, so 
as to keep the landed value of these goods at US$ 27.97 per 
kg. 
(ii) Tariff barriers to imports have been readjusted. In the Union 
budget of 8th July, 2004 the Finance Minister has declared an 
effective import tariff, including CVD and cess, on silk yarn and 
silk fabric of 30.192%. Duty on import of silk worm cocoon and 
raw silk has been kept at 30%. 
(iii) Several programmes and sc hemes to increase the quality, 
productivity and the competitiveness of the domestic silk 
industry have been instituted. The import ones are:— 
* Research and Development efforts of Central Silk Board have 
been stepped up to improve quantity and productivity of 
sericulture, by evolution of more productive and stress tolerant 
breeds and hybrids of mulberry and non-mulberry food plants 
and silkworms; and development of low cost reeling and 
processing technologies in silk; 
* Seed Support & Technical Assistance is being given by the 
Central Silk Board to State Governments, farmers & reelers 
7

by maintenance of parent races and basic seed, supply of 
commercial seed, and augmentation of grainage facilities 
for production of disease free high yielding and drought 
resistant seeds; 
* Central assistance is being exte nded to states through Cen- 
trally Sponsored & Central sector schemes to strengthen 
farm infrastructure, increase area under sericulture, upgrade 
reeling facilities, improve finishing processes, strengthen 
seed supply cocoon & silk testing systems; 
* Low cost and productivity enhancing technologies developed 
by the Central Silk Board are being popularized through 
central assistance to beneficiaries, training to the States' 
extension machinery and beneficiaries, organizing of 
various awareness programmes, etc; 
* For technology upgradation of the indigenous silk industry 
loan at 5% point less than the applicable bank rate, under 
the Technological Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) is 
available inter alia to silk sector. 
* Under the Swarnjayanti Gram Sw arojgar Yojana (SGSY) of 
the Ministry of Rural Development financial assistance is 
being provided to various States for implementation of seri- 
culture projects of all varieties of silk with the technical 
assistance of CSB; 
* Supply chain issues between the farmers, raw silk 
producers and the weavers are being addressed by 
advocating contract farming models, price linked grading, etc. 
* Establishing quality certification systems for silkworm 
seeds, cocoons, yarn and fabric. 
* An amount of Rs. 450 crores has been provided in the Tenth 
Plan for the Sericulture sector to support the above strategy 
& programmes; 
* Export of value added silk items is being encouraged through 
assistance to exporters for participation in fairs and exhibi-

Private Participation in Rural Development 
*309. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether steps have been initiated by Government for rural develop- 
ment through private sector; 
(b) if so, which are the areas identified; and 
(c) what are the details of facilities, concessions given to the private 
sector in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI RAGHUVANSH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
29 

RAJYA SABHA [22 December, 2004] 
Statement 
The Ministry of Rural Development has approved two special projects 
for generation of self-employment with private participation. The areas 
covered by these projects and the deta ils of concession s/facilities offered 
to the private sector for these projects are indicated below: 
(i) Livelihood Advancement Busine ss School: The objective of the 
project is to identify and make available potential livelihood options 
for 35,000 below poverty line (BPL) youth in the age group of 18-35 
years and train them in skills acco rding to the market requirements, 
thereby working towards achieving the goal of poverty reduction. Dr. 
Reddy's Foundation is to implement the project in 7 States. The 
total cost of the project is Rs. 14 crore, out of which the Government 
share is 75 per cent. 
(ii) Self-Help Group Mobilization,  Capacity Building and Credit 
Linkage: The objective of the project  is group mobilization, capacity 
building and credit linkage of the Self Help Groups (SHGs). ICICI 
Bank is to implement the project in two States at a total cost of Rs. 
15 crore. The Ministry of Rural Development would provide an amount 
of Rs. 10,000/- per SHG for social mobilization and Rs. 5,000/- per 
SHG for capacity building to ICICI Bank. 
2. While the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) is 
implemented by the State Governments, the works are executed by 
contractors who are generally in th e private sector. The contracts are 
awarded through well established tende ring procedures. In addition, the 
Ministry of Rural Development has signed a Memorandum of Understanding 
(MOU) with Shree Warana Rural Roads Development & Maintenance Co- 
operative Society Limited (WARANA) and Government of Maharashtra to 
enable the Society to execute PM GSY works in three districts of 
maharashtra. The MOU envisages planti ng of fruit trees by the Society on 
the sides of the roads and the revenu e from these trees would accrue to 
the Society. 
3. A National Fund for Rural Development (NFRD) also exists, to which 
individuals, corporate and non-corporate bodies can make donations. The 
NFRD is envisaged to act as a channel for mobilizing efforts and resources 
for rural development. The accruals to  the Fund are to be used for rural 
development projects, which may be implemented by the private sector 
also. Donations made by all categories of tax-payers to the National Fund 
for Rural Development are fully deductible from taxable income.

cation facilities and participates in long distance trunk telecommunication 
business venture.

mandated to catalyze Power Projects and Power Trading to optimally 
utilize the existing resources in the country as also promote exchange of

ment of hydro resources of Bhagirathi river and its tributaries at Tehri.

Sutlej Link Project and Pong Dam including Power Houses and a network

National Power Research. Organization and serves as a National Testing 
and Certification Authority for electrical equipments used in power sector. 
National Power Training Institute: The institute's main function is 
providing training for personnel in the Central and State utilities etc.

Review of Electricity Act 
2161. SHRIMATI MOHSINA KIDWAI: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Electricity Act, 2003 needs a review in order to have 
effective reforms in power sector; and 
(b) what are the views of Government with regard to incorporating provi- 
sions relating to open access, accountability to Regulatory Commission 
etc.? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) The National 
Common Minimum Programme of the Government states "The review of 
the Electricity Act, 2003 will be undertaken in view of the concern 
expressed by a number of States. The mandatory date of June, 10,2004 
for unbundling and replacing the State Electricity Boards will be extended". 
The mandatory date of June 10,2004 for unbundling of State Electricity 
Boards has been extended for periods ranging from 2 months to 12 months 
in respect of 13 States who had requested for such extension. Further, the 
State Transmission Utilities having authorization under the repealed 
electricity laws, have been authorized to engage in the activity of bulk 
purchase and sale of electricity to distribution companies for a further 
period of one year from 10th June, 2004. 
(b) The Electricity Act, 2003 provid es for open access in transmission 
from outset. Section 42 of the Act provides that the State Regulatory 
Commissions shall introdu ce open access in distribution in phases 
having due regard to all relevant factors including cross subsidy and other 
operational constraints. It further provides that open access to all 
consumers, who require a supply of electricty, where the maximum power 
to be made available at any time exceeds one megawatt, be provided not 
later than 27th January, 2009. 
As per the provisions of the Elect ricty Act, 2003, the licensees are 
accountable to Appropriate Regulatory Commission. One of the functions 
of the State Regulatory Commission und er the Act is to specify and 
enforce standards with respect to quality, quantum and reliability of 
service by licensees. A distribution licensee is also mandated under the 
137 

RAJYA SABHA [22 December, 2004] 
Act to establish a forum for redressal of grievances of consumers in accor- 
dance with the guidelines specified by the State Regulatory Commission. 
The Act also requires the State Commission to appoint/designate Om- 
budsman to look into non-redressal of consumers' grievances and settle 
the same within such time and in such manner as may be specified by the 
State Commission. 
Section 142 of the Act provides for punishment for non-compliance of 
directions issued by Appropriate Commission.

Steps for better economic condition of rural people 
2177. SHRI M.A.M RAMASWAMY: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that as per estimates 10 per cent of the total 
world population and 70 per cent of India's population lives in rural India; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that th e per capita income of the rural 
population is just Rs. 50 a day and this large population is isolated in 
terms of access to information, material and market; and 
(c) if so, the steps the Central Government has taken or propose to 
take to provide easy access to market  to the rural people and thus en- 
hance their economic condition? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOP- 
MENT (SHRIMATI SURYAKANTAPATIL): (a) According to one estimate 
52.3 per cent of the world population live in rural areas during 2004. 
According to Population Census 2001, the rural population of India is 72.22 
per cent. 
151 

RAJYA SABHA [22 December, 2004] 
(b) The available Statistics on National Income, as estimated by the 
Central Statistics Organisation, provide information on the per capita Net 
Domestic Product (NDP), separately for rural and urban areas at current 
prices at three points of time, viz 1970-71, 1980-81 and 1993-94. The 
annual per capita NDP in rural areas at national level has been estimated 
at Rs. 5783 in year 1993-94. The rural population is not isolated in terms 
of access to information, material and market. 
(c) The Ministry of Rural Development implements a self-employment 
scheme, namely, Swarnjayanti Gram Sw arozgar Yojana (SGSY) in all the 
rural areas of the country (except Ch andigarh and Delhi). The scheme has 
provisions of marketing infrastructure and mechanism for creating both 
forward and backward linkages. Trade fairs are also organized by the Min- 
istry to provide better marketing opportunities to improve socio-economic 
condition of the assisted swarozgar. 
Pooling of resources for development of non-forest wastelands 
2178. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of 
RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether involvement of private sector and financial institutions to 
pool resources for development of non-forest wastelands has been dis- 
continued; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the action taken to implement the recommendations made by the 
Parliamentary Standing Committee on the Ministry of Rural Development 
in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOP- 
MENT (SHRI A. NARENDRA): (a) to (c) The Investment Promotion 
Scheme, 
which was under implementation to promote development of non-forest 
wastelands through mobilization of resources from financial institutions, 
banks, corporate bodies and private land holders, was discontinued with 
effect from April, 2003 due to lack of adequate response from the promoter 
agencies/land holders. This was largely due to lack of a clear-cut policy in 
the States of leasing out of large chu nks of wastelands to private sector 
agencies and the comparatively attr active incentives including subsidy 
available to land holders in other land development schemes. In response 
to the recommendations made by the Parliamentary standing committee, 
the Committee has been apprised of these bottlenecks.

Special scheme for development of land and conservation of 
water 
†2181. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI : Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are consideri ng to start any special scheme 
for the development of land, protection from drought and flood and conser- 
vation of water; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) how far this programme is different from the programme of 'food for 
work'; and 
(d) by when the scheme is likely to be implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOP- 
MENT (SHRI A. NARENDRA): (a) to (d) The Ministry of Rural Develop- 
ment has launched a new poverty alleviation programme namely the Na- 
tional Food for Work Programme (NFFWP) with 100% funding during the 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
159 

RAJYA SABHA [22 December, 2004] 
current financial year i.e. 2004-05 from the month of November, 2004 in 
150 most backward districts of the country to generate additional supple- 
mentary wage employment with food security. All the States except Goa 
have been covered under the programme. The programme is open to all 
rural poor who are in need of wage employment and desire to do manual 
and unskilled work. Foodgrains to the States are also provided free of 
cost. During the current financial year i.e. 2004-05, the allocation under 
this programme is Rs. 2020 crore cash component and 20 lakh tonnes of 
foodgrains. The focus of the programme will be on works relating to water 
conservation, drought proofing (including afforestation/tree plantation) and 
land development. Flood control/protection (including drainage in water- 
logged areas), rural connectivity in terms of all weather roads and other 
similar activity for economic sustainability, keeping in view the area spe- 
cific problems, may also be taken up. 
The erstwhile Food for Work Programme (FFWP) was under operation 
between January 2001 to March 2002. Under this programme, only 
foodgrains were provided to the calamity  affected areas in order to provide 
additional supplementary wage employment to minimize hardship. The 
cash component of wages and material cost was to be met by the con- 
cerned State Governments from their own resources under various ongo- 
ing developmental/welfare schemes. As such the scheme was to be imple- 
mented through convergence/dovetaili ng with other programmes. But the 
NFFWP is a compact scheme having resources for both the components 
of the wages (cash and foodgrains) an d cash component for material cost 
as well. Besides, the NFFWP is allocation based programme whereas 
FFWP was demand driven.

Online computerised land information system 
2188. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will th e Minister of RURAL DEVELOP- 
MENT be pleased to state the details of steps taken or proposed to be 
taken for updating of land records, modernization of land record manage- 
ment system and their simultaneous computerization so that online com- 
puterized land information system could be developed in the country within 
a reasonable span of time to eliminate corruption and protecting illiterate 
farmers from exploitation? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE FOR RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI A. 
NARENDRA): Ministry of Rural Development has accorded high priority 
for improving land records management system in the country. Accord- 
ingly, two Centrally sponsored schemes i.e., Strengthening of Revenue 
Administration & Updating of Land Records (SRA & ULR) and Computer- 
ization of Land Records (CLR) are under implementation in States/Union 
Territories. Under the scheme of SRA & ULR, funds are provided to States 
on 50:50 sharing basis between Centre and States for carrying out survey/ 
revisonal survey with the use of mode rn technology to keep their records 
updated. Funds are also provided to States for strengthening of survey & 
settlement institutions and imparting training to Revenue Officials on lat- 
est techniques & tools for modernization of Revenue Administration and 
regular updation of land records. 
The scheme of Computerzation of Land Records (CLR) was started 
in 1988-89 with 100% financial support from Govt. of India with the aim of 
ensuring accuracy, efficiency, transp arency and removing Inherent flaws 
in the existing land records maintenance system. The main objective of 
the scheme of CLR is that land owners should get updated computerized 
copies of their Record of Rights on demand from the taluk/tehsil computer 
centres. The scheme aims to carry out regular updation of land records 
through automation of mutation workflow. So far the scheme has been 
sanctioned in 582 districts of the country and it has been extended to 
3236 taluks/tehsils/blocks and 471 sub-divisions.

Fall in prices of cotton 
2195. SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JO SHI: Will the Minister of 
TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the prices of cotton are falling unprecedently; 
(b) if so, the reasons for the down fall in prices and action proposed by 
Government to arrest this fall; 
(c) whether Government intends to rope in Cotton Corporation of India 
to purchase cotton at MSP; if not, the reasons therefor; and   - 
(d) whether Government intends to compensate the cotton farmers who 
have sold their produce at distressed prices? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA): 
(a) 
Kapas (seed cotton) prices during the first two and half months of the 
current cotton year (October 2004 to September 2005) has ruled lower by 
7%-28% ttan the prices prevailing during the corresponding period last 
year. Cotton prices in global market  during the current cotton year are 
also ruling lower than the prices prevailing during the corresponding period 
last year. 
(b) Higher domestic as well as global  cotton production is the primary 
reason for low prices of cotton. The cotton prices during the year 2003-04 
were unusually hi gh (25-30% above the prices in the preceding year 2002- 
03) because of low global producti on (20.61 Million MT) and higher con- 
sumption (21,34 Million MT). Therefore,  lower prices during the current 
year as compared to last year ar e on the expected line. Whenever the 
market prices of Kapas fall to the level of the Minimum Support Price 
(MSP) declared by the Central Government, the Cotton Corporation of 
India (CCI) undertakes MSP operati ons and procures Kapas without any 
quantitative limit. During the current cotton season, the CCI has under- 
taken MSP operations in several States as a result of which prices of 
cotton have not fallen below the MSP level. 
(c) The CCI has already co mmenced MSP operations  in the States of 
Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, 
Punjab and Rajasthan. Till 10.12.2004, the CCI has purchased 20,58,420 
quintals of Kapas (equivalent to lint cotton of 3,92,080 bales of 170 kg. 
each). 
(d) The cotton growers have been ensured remunerative price through 
MSP operations by the CCI whenever the market price of Kapas has fallen 
to the level of the MSP.

Policy to tap youth energy 
2209. SHRI AJAY SINGH CHAUTALA : Will the Minister of YOUTH 
AFFAIRS AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to frame a policy to harness the en- 
ergy of youths and also to give them a direction so that their talent and 
merits should not go waste and remain idle; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; and 
(d) when it would be implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI SUNIL 
DUTT): (a) to (d) National Youth Policy, 2003 is under implementation for 
utilizing the energy of youth and motivating them to be active and commit- 
ted participants in the exciting task of National Development. The Policy 
identifies following thrust areas:- 
(i) Youth Empowerment; 
(ii) Gender Justice; 
(Hi) Inter-Sectoral Approach; 
(iv) Information and Research Network. 
187 

RAJYA SABHA [22 December, 2004] 
12.00 Noon 
The Policy recognizes eight key sectors of concern for the youth viz. 
(a) Education, (b) Training and Employment, (c) Health and Family 
Welfare, (d) Preservation of Environmen t, Ecology and Wildlife, (e) Recre- 
ation and Sports, (f) Arts and Culture, (g) Science and Technology and (h) 
Civics and good Citizenship. 
Under the National Youth Policy, 2003 a National Inter-departmental 
Committee under the Chairpersonship of  Secretary has been constituted 
to prepare draft National Action Plan for the implementation of the Policy. 
Adolescents have been recognized  as a major segment under the 
National Youth Policy. The Ministry has formulated and launched a Scheme 
for Development and Empowerment of Adolescents, in the age group of 
10—19 years. Under this scheme, non-governmental organisations, 
educational institutions etc., are being assisted to undertake projects and 
programmes relating to issues concerning adolescents. 
The Ministry has taken a large number of initiatives to strengthen Youth 
Clubs under Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathan (NYKS). These include 
expanding their membership to cover adolescents, launching of Gandhi 
Gramodya Sankalp Abhiyan, introduction of the concept of Rural 
Connectivity 
through Information Technology, emphasis on Vocational Training etc. In 
this regard, the Ministry has sought convergence with other Ministries/ 
Departments like Human Resource Development, Rural Development Health 
and Family Welfare. Women and Child Development and Culture to promote 
youth development and their involvement in national development.

Need to bring Gannavaram Telephone Exchange under 
Vijayawada Digital Exchange in Andhra Pradesh 
SHRIK RAMA MOHANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Chairman, Sir, 
my Special Mention is pertaining to bring Gannavaram Telephone Exchange 
under Vijayawada Digital Exchange. 
Sir, Gannavaram is having more t han 3,000 working-connections and is 
served with RSU. It is, in turn connected to MBM Exchange at Vuyyuru, 
since it falls under Vuyyuru Short Dis tance Charging Area. Due to routing 
of STD/|SD calls through Vuyyuru SD CA, which is about 50 Kms. from 
Gannavaram, the people are facing umpteen problems. The point is, 
Gannavaram is just 16 Kms. away fr om Vijayawada and Vuyyuru is about 
50 Kms. 
[MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN in the Chair] 
Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I faiied to understand the rationale in routing 
the calls through Vuyyuru where the distance is 50 Kms. and not routing 
through Vijayawada which is just 16 Kms. away! There is also no techni- 
cal or any other problem to give the STD Code of Vijayawada to 
Gannavaram, since it is closer to Vijayawada than Vuyyuru. I don't under- 
stand why the calls are not routed through Vijayawada, which is just , 
16 Kms away. 
I had also raised this on the floor of the House on 21st August, 2001, 
through a supplementary to Questi on No. 403. The then Minister had 
assured that Gannavaram Exchange in  Krishna District of Andhra Pradesh 
would be brought under Vijayawada Digital Exchange within three to four 
months. But, so far, nothing has been done in this regard.  
I also wish to bring to the notice of the Government of India that 
Gannavaram comes under Vijayawada Municipal limits and it also comes 
under the jurisdiction of Police Commissionerate of Vijayawada. Hence, I 
implore upon the Government of Indi a to immediately bring Gannavaram 
Exchange under Vijayawada digital exchange.

SHRI S.P.M. SYED KHAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, Article 351 of our Consti- 
tution talkt about the promotion of Hindi  language so that it may serve as 
a medium of expression for all the el ements of the composite culture of 
India. Hindi, of course, is the India' s official language and taught in all 
parts of the country. Now-a-days, many  schools in South India also widely 
teaching Hindi considering its import ance as the National Language as 
also for the sake of patriotism. There is no doubt that Hindi is a beautiful 
language but then so are the Dravidian languages. Now, the situation is

that a large number of South Indian s could speak Hindi whereas the Hindi 
belt does not, in any way, feel oblig ated to speak a South Indian language. 
National unity comes through frequent Inter-mixing of people, the language, 
and the culture. From Kashmir to Ka nyakumari, we are bound by many 
things. But one this is missing i.e., linguistic assimilation. Now, the South 
Indian States are rapidly making progress in the field of education, 
industrialisation and technology. The South Indian inst itutes have become 
very popular in the country and employment opportunities have also in- 
creased in the Southern India. It would be a unique contribution to the 
genuine enhancement of national integrat ion if the millions of school chil- 
dren in the North India are familiarized with a South Indian language. 
I would, therefore, urge upon the Go vernment to consider teaching a 
South Indian language i.e., Tamil, Telugu, Kannada or Malyalam in the 
schools of the North Indi a under the Three Language Formula, which would, 
no doubt, enhance the national integration to a greater extent.

University, Orissa 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR (Orissa): Sir, it  is gratifying to learn that the 
Government is considering the Allahabad  University for grant of the Cen- 
tral University status. The Human Resource Development Minister has 
introduced a Bill to this effect. 
In this context, may I mention, Sir,  that granting of Central University 
status to the Sambalpur University is  also under the consideration of the 
Government for quite sometime. The Go vernment of Orissa, during Janu- 
ary this year, has already sent its recommendation to make the Sambalpur 
University a Central University.

The Sambalpur University, establish ed in 1967, caters to the higher 
educational needs of one of  the most backward regi ons of the State. Most 
parts of the Kalahandi-Bol angir-Koraput, that is, KBK districts are covered 
by this university, devoting to the education of tribal and underprivileged 
students. Since its establishment, t he Sambalpur University has shown 
excellence in academic result and research work. It has 184 affiliated

knowledge, like Biotechnology, Com puter Science, Earth Science are

ment is keen and sincere to develop the backward areas, granting the 
Central University status to the Sambalpur University will be a benevolent 
step towards it. Thank you.

Demand for taking urgent measures for Protecting Environment 
in the Country 
SHRIMATI SYEDA ANWARA TAIMUR (Assam): Mr. Deputy Chair- 
man, Sir, ws are living in the world of science and technology, but, simul- 
taneously, pollution has become a burning problem in the world. In our 
country, it is one of the serious problems. The National Highways 
Authority of India has decided to conv ert national highways from two-lane 
roads to four-lane roads. And, I have seen a large number of big, matured 
roadside trees being cut and removed for broadening the two-lane roads 
by the National Highways Authority of India. 
Now, many countries have got the technology for uprooting matured 
tress and planting them, wherever it is needed for plantation. 
If we plant new plants in place of those cut, it may take a long time to 
grow them, which may affect the environment. 
So, I urge upon the Government to start the technology of uprooting 
matured trees and to plant them somewhere, instead of cutting them. 
214

Big and small cities should have a sewage system. Many cities are 
running without a sewage system. Before declaring a town as a city, it 
should be provided with a proper sewage system. The Central and State 
Pollution Boards are constituted, but to our knowledge, they are not strict in 
this regard. I think, the Government sh ould pay more attention in this regard 
so that it can help in bringing down the level of pollution to some extent. 
Maintaining a proper sewage system is not only hygienic and good for the 
health of the society, but it will also prevent cont amination of fresh ground 
water. 
I, therefore, urge upon the Governmen t, through you, Sir, to pay more 
attention in this regard to protect the environment. 
Need to revive the Hindustan Photo Films at Ooty in Tamil Nadu 
SHRI THANGA TAMIL SELVAN (Tamil Na du): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I 
want to bring to the notice of the Government the need to revive the Hindustan 
Photo Films at Oooty in Tamil Nadu. Th ere, are a very few Central Public 
Undertakings in Tamil Nadu, and the Hindustan Photo Films is one of them. It 
is one of the old PSUs which was start ed in 1967. The decision of the Centre 
to close down this factory, taken on 25.08.2004, has put a question mark on 
the future of the employees. There are over 1000 employees in the factory, 
with their families dependent on them. The reason of non-viability, as stated 
by the Government, is not correct because this Company was given ISO 
2001 Certificate in the year  2000. While the market potential of the photo- 
graphic films in India is over Rs. 1300/- crore a year, the Hindustan Photo 
Films has not been adequately modernis ed to have a competitive edge. Even 
the operating cash-toss has come down  from Rs. 30.26 crore in 1997-98 to 
Rs. 10.28 crore in 2003-04. If the Centre provides policy support in the 
fields of Healthcare, Defence, etc. under its management, then Hindustan 
Photo Films can have additional turnover to the tune of Rs. 350 crores. 
The amount required for the revival of this factory is only Rs. 250 crore. 
Providing this fund will save the live lihood of over 1000 families and will 
also create more job opportunities in the factory and around. It will start 
earning profit very soon and will develop into a big industry. In view of this, 
I appeal to the Central Government to allocate Rs. 250 crore for the revival 
of Hindustan Photo Films, Ooty and save the livelihood of employees.

Concern over the plight of the small scale industries in the 
country 
SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR (Maharashtra ): Sir, the small scale indus- 
try in India has proved to be a very big engine of growth for the Indian 
economy. The small scale industry accounts for 40 per cent of the indus- 
trial production, 36 per cent of India' s exports and it provides nearly 60 per 
cent of the industrial employment. The total turnover of SSI in India is 
above Rs. 7,50,000 crores which is equ al to above 25 per cent of India's 
GDP. 
The issues concerning bank credit to small-scale industries continue 
to be left unattended by negligence of the RBI, in spite of reports of several 
specialised Committees like the Nayak Committee (1991-1992), Abid 
Hussain Committee (1998), and S.L Kapur Committee (1998). Adequate 
credit, on the basis of 20 per cent of  the projected annual turnover, is not 
provided by the banks to SSIs. Very high rates of interest, i.e. from 14 per 
cent per annum to 16 per cent per an num, continue to be charged to-SSIs. 
though bank credit is available to the large scale industry in India at 6 per 
cent per annum, to 9 per cent per annum. Though there is a recommenda- 
218 

[22 December, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
tion by the SSI Ministry of the Government of India that credit should be 
made available to SSIs in a 2 per cent band, above or below the PLR of 
banks, the RBI does not ensur e that banks follow this policy and, in fact, 
no bank follows this policy in actual practice. 
All these drawbacks have resulted in rampant sickness in small-scale 
industries. From about 23,000 sick un its in 1980, the number of sick SSIs 
has increased to 2,18,000 in 1990, and today, in 2004, there are 3,60,000 
sick SSI units in India. Several lakh SSI units have closed shops. 
I request all the concerned Ministries  in the Government of India to 
shake up and wake up the RBI to the pi tiable plight of the SSI sector. Sir, 
I express my happiness that the hon. Finance Minister is present here. 
Thank you.

Need to control population in the country 
SHRI DARA SINGH (Nominated): Indi a today ranks first in the total 
number of child deaths, with 2.4 millio n dying before the age of five whereas 
China with a higher population base, ranks third with 0.78 million child 
deaths. It is a fact that good health of a mother alon e can give birth to a 
healthy child. China had controlled its population by introducing strict 
laws which have helped them to becom e a healthy nation, and its young 
sportsmen have surprised the whole world by winning a good number of 
gold medals in recently held Olympi c games. We also have the potential 
to become a great nation only if we control the population explosion 
because otherwise the fruits of development will never be real. So far, our 
policies and programmes to control the population in the country have 
failed. My humble suggestion to the Central Govenment is to make strict 
laws like China, as without laws, we cannot control the population. I wish 
our nation may become a healthy and an educated one, and our sports-

co-operation, both bilateral as well as within the context of the African 
Union and India's contributions to peace-keeping Missions in several 
African countries, all reflect this desire. The announcement by our 
President, while visiting Sourth Africa in September, 2004, of an ambitious 
project for linking all 53 African countri es through a satellite as well as a 
fibre optic based network, is reflective of our resolve to contribute to 
African development. 
Central Asia is part of our extended neighbourhood. Besides the 
longstanding historical and cultural lin kages, we also see Central Asia as 
an important economic partner as po inted out by Dr. Karan Singh, 
particularly in terms of our energy re quirements. We are, therefore, moving 
quickly to intensify our relations with the countries of the region through 
high level visits and increased economic and commercial interactions. 
Intensified relations with Latin Amer ica and the Caribbean are reflected 
in the Ministerial visits of Foreign Mi nisters of Mexico, Venezuela, Surinam, 
and, the visit of Minister of State fo r External Affairs, Shri Rao Inderjit 
Singh to Panama, Columbia, Dominican Republic and El Salvador. Early 
during the next year, we hope to host  the President of Chile; and, the 
Vice-President of Surinam would be coming as the Chief Guest for the 
PravasiBharatiya Diwas next month, reflecting t he linkages that India has 
with the region. Our collaboration with Brazil on the Security Council re- 
form, and, in the WTO reflects the growth in our commonalities with this 
Latin American giant. These initiatives taken by the UPA Government 
should allay the apprehensions expres sed by some members that we are 
neglecting the Latin American and Caribbean regions; we are not. 
Let me now turn to the United Nations. The efforts of the UPA Govern- 
ment have ensured that India's claim today to be a permanent member of 
the Security Council within the cont ext of overall reform of the UN has 
been well established within the international community. Intensive 
displomacy on our part has resulted in the creation of a common platform 
of the four most credible aspirant s for permanent membership of the 
Security Council. India, Brazil, Germany and Japan who are mutually 
supportive of each other, have agree d to work together to realize their 
shared objective. We also support African representation in the 
295 

RAJYA SABHA [22 December, 2004] 
permanent membership in an expanded Security Council, if and when it 
takes place. 
Recently, the panel appointed by t he UN Secretary General on 'Threats, 
Challenges and Change" has submitted a number of recommendations on 
institutional changes in the UN, in cluding the composition of the UN 
Security Council. We are studying them, and, in consultation with other 
Member States, we will decide how to take the process of reform forward 
during the next year; next year being the 60th anniversary of the founding 
of the United Nations. It was hoped that the reforms and restructuring 
could take place in 1995 at the 50th anniversary, but it didn't happen. 
Before I conclude, I would now like to say a few words on some of the 
doubts and misgivings expressed in the House on our claim for a perma- 
nent seat in the UN Security Council. The Prime Minister himself stated 
yesterday and I quote: 
"There is no confusion regarding our  position on our candidature for a 
permanent seat in the Security Council. At this point, all permanent 
members have veto powers. We are a candidate. The issue may arise in 
respect of any new permanent members who may be admitted. Our 
fundamental position remains clear. We do not believe that there should 
be any discrimination in the Security Council and there should be no 
distinction between permanent members who have veto and those who 
don't. This position is based on the broadest possible political consen- 
sus". We intend to press home this position vigorously in the days to 
come. 
Doubts were raised as to whether under the UPA Government India- 
Russia relations have received some kind of a setback, and, I am saying 
this in the context of what happened during President Putin's visit. 
President Putin's remarks, at a joint press conference with our Prime 
Minister, were unfortunately misinterpr eted by some journalists who thought 
he was implying that new permanent members to the Security Council 
would not enjoy veto status. This was set right by President Putin himself 
in very categorical terms the very next day, and, I happened to be there 
when he made this observation to the Press. When I said, "Thank you, 
Mr. President", and, he said, "No, it was very necessary for me because I 
thought I had made myself clear on the first day". Obviously, there was 
something wrong in the translation. 
Here again, we should avoid the pr opensity to swallow what the foreign 
policy experts, hidden and not so hidden, pronounced on such important

the Cabinet Committee on Security, of which you had been a distinguished

new direction keeping in view political and economic changes that are 
taking place in our region. And, with your permission, Sir, I would like to 
quote a very distinguished Europ ean Statesman, Richard Weizsacker, 
President of Germany for ten years. In  his Nehru Memorial Lecture this is 
what he said. And Germany was not a non-aligned country. "Nehru was 
among the first and the foremost to lo ok for a non-bloc internationalism. 
His idea of non-alignment became a gl obal importance. He spoke about 
peace clubs against cold-war clubs, nuclear clubs. He was pondering how 
to create a sort of no-war land betwee n the military blocs. From the but- 
set, his thoughts became and remained fruitful. Non-alignment was aim- 
ing at more than distance to blocs. It was a denial of the gist of bloc- 
thinking, an endeavour to detect inside those blocs growing trends of open- 
ness, of looking for common interests,  of conditions how to survive to- 
gether, of detente policy recommended and practised by leaders like Willy 
Brandt, of arms control and arms reduction proposals, such as Pugwash 
Conference ideas which served later at initiatives for the SALT Agreement 
and the like. Nehru's non-aligned pol icy is not a means to prevent 
co-operation. It is, on the co ntrary, an invitation never to give up the search 
for new ways leading to peaceful co-existence, detente and reconciliation. 
Sir, obviously, the international ag enda has changed. So, naturally, the 
agenda of the Non-Aligned Movement has changed. But, let us not mix up 
the Non-Aligned Movement with non-alignment. Non-alignment is good for 
ever. The Non-Aligned Movement has to address itself to the problems like 
terrorism, drugs, HIV AIDS, financial cr ises, population control, environ- 
ment and, here, the Non-Aligned Move ment needs diplomatic blood trans- 
fusion, and we intend to give it as much as we can, within our limitations. 
There are so many other members. The original members, Indonesia, 
Yugoslavia, Egypt, are not so active in the Non-Aligned Movement. But I 
•think the Non-Aligned Movement rema ins relevant for the rest as non- 
alignment.

pledge and given us a foreign policy which is purposeful, result-oriented 
and pro-active. While it ias been the endeavour of this Government to 
follow the basic principle's of our foreign policy which have guided India
